sections.h2: Which Washington County offices handle a property tax bill?
sections.html:
The Assessor of Property values the land and buildings, the County Commission picks the rate, and the Trustee collects. The Trustee's page is blunt about it: the Trustee only collects, and has no role in appraisals or in setting the rate. Value questions go to the Assessor at 423-753-1671.

The Trustee, Rick Storey, runs two counters. The Jonesborough office is in the Historic Courthouse downtown, phone 423-753-1602, open weekdays 8 to 4:30, with a drop box at the corner of the courthouse. The Johnson City office is at 378 Marketplace Boulevard, phone 423-610-7211, with hours of 8:30 to 4:30 listed from November 3, 2025. Mail goes to PO Box 215, Jonesborough, TN 37659.

The county bill does not cover everything. The Trustee notes that homes in Johnson City or the Town of Jonesborough also owe city property tax, so a house inside either one gets more than one bill.

sections.h2: What is Washington County like, and how does that show up in values?
sections.html:
Washington County is the oldest county in Tennessee, set up in 1777 while the area still belonged to North Carolina. Jonesborough is the county seat and is called Tennessee's oldest town. Johnson City, the largest city, started as a railroad depot and is now home to East Tennessee State University and a regional medical center. The county covers 330 square miles, with the Nolichucky River crossing the south and the Watauga River along the north.

Ridges and valleys fill the west, while the Blue Ridge side rises in the east toward Buffalo Mountain and the Cherokee National Forest. Interstates 26 and 81 both cross the county. Two public school systems serve it: Washington County Schools, and Johnson City Schools for most of that city. Gray, Telford, Fall Branch and Oak Grove are census-designated places outside the two main towns.

Census Bureau QuickFacts for Washington County:

  • 141,199 residents in July 2025, up 6.2% from April 2020
  • 64,564 housing units, with 64.5% owner-occupied
  • Median owner-occupied home value of $249,000 for 2020 to 2024
  • Median household income of $62,809, and a mean commute of 21.6 minutes
  • 697 building permits in 2025

One local wrinkle: after the Hurricane Helene flooding of 2024, the Assessor's office asked affected owners to return a reassessment form so values could be adjusted.

sections.h2: How does Washington County calculate the tax on a house?
sections.html:
The Trustee spells out three steps: take the appraised value, multiply by 25 percent for residential property (40 percent for commercial), then multiply the result by the rate for each $100. The county's example is a $150,000 home, which becomes $37,500 of assessed value and a bill of $806.25. Since tax year 2020 the County Commission rounds bills to the nearest dollar, so that example reads $806.

The rate on the Trustee's page is $2.15 per $100, labeled as the 2023 county rate. Run on a home at the Census median of $249,000, the county tax would be about $1,338 a year at that rate. Confirm the current figure with the Trustee before relying on it. The rate splits among these funds:

FundRate per $100 assessedSource
County General$0.79Washington County Trustee
General Purpose School$0.74Washington County Trustee
Debt Service$0.25Washington County Trustee
Education Capital Projects$0.17Washington County Trustee
Highway$0.135Washington County Trustee
Sanitation, Capital Projects$0.035 and $0.03Washington County Trustee
Total$2.15Washington County Trustee

Schools take the largest slice, roughly $0.91 of the $2.15 once education capital is counted with the general purpose school rate.

sections.h2: When is Washington County property tax due, and what if the notice never arrives?
sections.html:
Notices usually go out in October and the tax is payable through the end of February. A balance still open on March 1 gets 1.5 percent interest, added each month. The Trustee wants taxes paid on time whether or not a notice shows up, and asks anyone who has not received one by November 15 to call. That date is today, so an owner without a bill, other than a mortgage escrow customer, should phone 423-753-1602 now.

The Trustee's payment options are:

  • In person at the Jonesborough or Johnson City office, or in the drop boxes at either one
  • Online at washington.paytntaxes.com, entering the tax year and bill number
  • By phone at 1-855-777-3468, or by e-check from a personal account

The Trustee also allows partial and prepaid payments, handled at the two offices. A 2021 notice from the office said unpaid balances after the delinquency period move to the Clerk and Master for collection, so ask the Trustee how that date works for the current year before letting a bill slide.

sections.h2: How can a Washington County owner appeal an assessment?
sections.html:
The Assessor opens the assessment roll for public inspection in May and mails notice to owners whose values changed. Owners who think a value exceeds fair market value can appeal, and the County Board of Equalization hears those cases and makes the roll final. Call 423-753-1671 to ask about the board's schedule and to request an informal look at the value.

The state backs up the local board. An owner unhappy with its decision can file with the State Board of Equalization by August 1 of the tax year or 45 days after the county board's notice went out, whichever is later. The state advises paying at least the undisputed part of the bill on time. Evidence the state favors includes recent sales of similar homes and a professional appraisal, along with a stated value. The hearing is held before an administrative judge, and the owner has the burden of proof.

sections.h2: What tax relief programs apply in Washington County?
sections.html:
The state Tax Relief Program began in 1973 and reimburses qualified elderly and disabled homeowners, as well as disabled veterans and their surviving spouses. The Trustee says Washington County matches the state amount, up to the amount billed. A veteran rated 100 percent disabled qualifies, and the relief passes to a surviving spouse. Relief is not an exemption, so the bill is paid first.

Applicants bring a driver's license, Medicare card, Social Security card and proof of the previous year's income. The state sends the income threshold to the Trustee in November. Other counties list the 2026 cap as $38,470 on 2025 income, so ask the Trustee in Washington County to confirm. A voucher has to be returned each year or the relief lapses for that year.

sections.h2: What should I know about property tax when selling in Washington County?
sections.html:
State law fixes the official tax roll as of January 1, so the person on the roll that day is the owner of record for the whole year. The Trustee usually tries to mail a notice to the new owner after a sale, because the office cannot know who agreed to pay. Taxes are normally prorated at closing, with the buyer made the responsible party, and a buyer who gets no notice is told to call and check the parcel.

A seller carrying an unpaid balance can ask the Trustee for the exact payoff, including any interest, before closing. The title company then builds that figure into the settlement statement. Things to line up before a sale:

  • The tax year and bill number for each parcel, which are needed to pay online
  • Any relief voucher that has not yet been returned for the year
  • Whether a city bill from Johnson City or Jonesborough is also open

An owner who plans to sell a house that was flooded in 2024 should also ask the Assessor whether the reassessment was completed, since a lower value changes what the buyer will owe next year.

faqs.q: What is the property tax rate in Washington County, TN?
faqs.a: The Trustee's page lists $2.15 per $100 of assessed value as the county rate. Homes in Johnson City or Jonesborough also pay city tax.

faqs.q: Where do I pay Washington County property tax?
faqs.a: Pay at the Jonesborough office in the Historic Courthouse or the Johnson City office at 378 Marketplace Boulevard. Online and phone payment also work.

faqs.q: What if I never received my Washington County tax notice?
faqs.a: Call the Trustee at 423-753-1602. The office asks owners to call if no notice has arrived by November 15, and owners are expected to pay on time either way.

faqs.q: How is Washington County property tax calculated?
faqs.a: Multiply the appraised value by 25 percent for a home, then multiply by $2.15 per $100. A $150,000 home works out to $806.

faqs.q: Who sets my home's value in Washington County?
faqs.a: The Assessor of Property does, at 423-753-1671. The Trustee only collects the tax.
